---
title: "Joining and Summarizing Data in SQL"
---


::: {.learning-objectives}
## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Join tables with INNER JOIN on their logical keys, using table aliases, and test that the keys match before relying on the result.
2. Use LEFT JOIN to keep rows that have no match, and to find the records that have none.
3. Summarize rows with aggregate functions, GROUP BY, and HAVING, grouping by key rather than by name.
4. Recognize fan-out when a join repeats a header's amount on every line, and avoid the double counting it causes.
5. Write subqueries in the WHERE and FROM clauses to answer questions that take more than one step.
6. Build a trial balance from the general ledger and follow a cost through the ledger with joined and grouped queries.
:::


## Opening Scenario {.unnumbered}

Your queries in Chapter 9 gave the controller a first look at the manufacturing variance. It is recorded when a work order closes, and in the largest closes of fiscal 2026 most of it is overhead. She has three follow-up questions. Which products carry the variance? How much of it arose in each of the three years? And is it a matter of volume, with the plant making fewer units over which to spread its costs, or of the cost itself?

None of these questions can be answered from one table. The product is recorded on the work order, not on its close. The cost of labor is recorded in the payroll, and the output in the production completions. The ledger holds the amounts, but it identifies accounts only by their AccountID. Answering the controller means joining these tables on the keys you studied in Chapter 3 and summarizing thousands of their rows into a few totals. This chapter teaches both skills, and it ends with an answer to her third question.



## Why Join Tables

A relational database stores each fact once, in the table where it belongs, and links the tables through keys. A work order close records its variance and the WorkOrderID of the work order it closes. The work order records the ItemID of the item it makes, and the Item table records the item's name and group. To see the variance by product group, you must follow those links, from the close to the work order and from the work order to the item. In SQL, following a link is called a join.

You have met the idea twice already. Chapter 3 introduced primary keys, foreign keys, and the cardinality of each relationship, and Chapter 5 used Power Query's Merge command to combine the invoice lines with the invoices, items, and customers. A join is the SQL version of that merge. It matches rows from two tables whose key values are equal and returns a result that combines columns from both.

One point from Chapter 3 matters more here than anywhere else. The Charles River database declares no foreign keys, so nothing guarantees that every WorkOrderID in WorkOrderClose matches a work order. The relationships are logical and must be tested. A join on keys that do not match does not fail with an error. It simply returns fewer rows, or more, than you expected, so every join in this chapter is checked by comparing the number of rows it returns with the number it should return.


## Inner Joins

An inner join returns one row for each pair of rows, one from each table, whose keys match. You write it in the FROM clause, with INNER JOIN and an ON condition that names the matching columns:

```sql
SELECT woc.WorkOrderCloseID, woc.CloseDate, wo.WorkOrderNumber,
    wo.ItemID, woc.TotalVarianceAmount
FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
    INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID;
```

The short names after AS are table aliases. Once a table has an alias, every column that comes from it is written with the alias and a period, as in `woc.CloseDate`. Aliases keep queries short, and they are required whenever a column name appears in both tables. WorkOrderID is a column of both WorkOrderClose and WorkOrder, so a query that asks for WorkOrderID without saying which table it comes from stops with the message ambiguous column name: WorkOrderID. The queries in this book qualify every column in a join, even when its name is unique, so that a reader can see where each one comes from.

A join can continue through several tables, one INNER JOIN at a time. Adding the Item table brings the item's code, name, and group onto each close:

```sql
SELECT woc.WorkOrderCloseID, woc.CloseDate, i.ItemCode, i.ItemName,
    i.ItemGroup, woc.TotalVarianceAmount
FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
    INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID
    INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = wo.ItemID;
```

Because every close belongs to exactly one work order, and every work order to exactly one item, this query should return exactly as many rows as the WorkOrderClose table holds. If it returns fewer, some closes point to a work order or an item that does not exist, and the inner join has dropped them without a word. Comparing the row count with the table's is the test of the keys.

@fig-10-01 shows how an inner join matches rows, using four work orders, three of them closed. The inner join returns the three that have a close. The fourth, which has not closed, has no match and does not appear. The lower half of the figure shows the left join, which the chapter turns to later.

![How Inner and Left Joins Match Rows.](/visuals/svg/fig-10-01-join-matching.svg){#fig-10-01 fig-alt="Four Charles River work orders on the left and the work order closes on the right, three of the work orders with a close and one without. The upper result, an inner join on WorkOrderID, holds three rows, one for each work order with a close. The lower result, a left join from WorkOrder, holds all four work orders, and the one without a close shows NULL in the close columns."}


## Summarizing with Aggregate Functions

An aggregate function calculates one value from many rows. @tbl-10-01 lists the five you will use most. Without a GROUP BY clause, an aggregate summarizes every row the query keeps, so `SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(TotalVarianceAmount) FROM WorkOrderClose` returns a single row with the number of closes and their total variance.

| Function | Returns | Treatment of NULL |
|---|---|---|
| `COUNT(*)` | The number of rows | Counts every row |
| `COUNT(column)` | The number of values in a column | Skips NULLs |
| `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` | The number of different values | Skips NULLs |
| `SUM(column)` | The total | Skips NULLs |
| `AVG(column)` | The average | Skips NULLs, so they do not count as zero |
| `MIN(column)`, `MAX(column)` | The smallest and largest values | Skip NULLs |

: Aggregate functions and how they treat missing values {#tbl-10-01}

GROUP BY divides the rows into groups that share the same values in the columns you name, and calculates each aggregate once per group. This query totals the variance of fiscal 2026 by item group:

```sql
SELECT i.ItemGroup, COUNT(*) AS Closes,
    ROUND(SUM(woc.TotalVarianceAmount), 2) AS TotalVariance
FROM WorkOrderClose AS woc
    INNER JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.WorkOrderID = woc.WorkOrderID
    INNER JOIN Item AS i ON i.ItemID = wo.ItemID
WHERE woc.CloseDate BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'
GROUP BY i.ItemGroup
ORDER BY TotalVariance DESC;
```

The result has one row for each item group, as @fig-10-02 illustrates. Every column in the SELECT list is either named in GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate function. A column that is neither has no single value for the group, and most database systems reject the query. SQLite does not: it accepts columns that are neither grouped nor aggregated and fills them with the value from one of the group's rows (SQLite, n.d.). That value says nothing about the group as a whole, so treat such a column as an error even though SQLite accepts it.

![GROUP BY Collapses Rows into One Row per Group.](/visuals/svg/fig-10-02-group-by.svg){#fig-10-02 fig-alt="On the left, several Charles River work order closes of fiscal 2026 with their item group and total variance, some from Furniture and some from Lighting. Arrows gather the rows of each group into one row of the result on the right, which shows each item group with the number of closes and the sum of their variances."}

You can group by more than one column. `GROUP BY i.ItemGroup, CloseYear` produces one row for each combination of group and year. The year of a close is not stored in its own column. A date stored as text in the form year-month-day begins with the year, however, so the text function `SUBSTR(woc.CloseDate, 1, 4)`, which returns the first four characters, gives it. Chapter 11 introduces SQLite's date functions, which do this and much more.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
Group by the key, not by the name. Two different Charles River customers are called Brown LLC, and several items share their names with other items. A query that groups by CustomerName combines the orders of both Brown LLCs into one row, and nothing in the result shows that it has done so. Group by CustomerID, and include the name in the GROUP BY clause as well if you want to show it.
:::

## Filtering Groups with HAVING

WHERE filters rows before they are grouped. HAVING filters the groups after the aggregates are calculated, so its condition can use them. To list only the accounts whose balance at the end of fiscal 2026 is not zero, you group the ledger rows by account and keep the groups whose total is not zero:

```sql
SELECT gl.AccountID, ROUND(SUM(gl.Debit) - SUM(gl.Credit), 2) AS Balance
FROM GLEntry AS gl
WHERE gl.PostingDate <= '2026-12-31'
GROUP BY gl.AccountID
HAVING ROUND(SUM(gl.Debit) - SUM(gl.Credit), 2) <> 0;
```

An aggregate cannot appear in a WHERE clause, because WHERE runs before any group exists. A query that tries it, such as one with `WHERE COUNT(*) > 5`, stops with the message misuse of aggregate: COUNT(). When a condition concerns single rows, such as a date range, it belongs in WHERE. When it concerns a group's total, count, or average, it belongs in HAVING. Filtering rows in WHERE also makes a query faster, because fewer rows reach the grouping step.


## Keeping Unmatched Rows with LEFT JOIN

An inner join keeps only matched rows. A left join keeps every row of the first table, the one named in FROM, and adds the columns of the second table where a match exists. Where none exists, those columns are NULL, as the lower half of @fig-10-01 shows. Left joins answer two kinds of question. The first is a complete list, such as every manufactured item with the number of work orders it has, including the items that have none. The second is an exception list: the rows that have no match at all.

The second kind is called an anti-join. You write a left join and keep only the rows where a column from the second table is NULL:

```sql
SELECT i.ItemCode, i.ItemName, i.ItemGroup
FROM Item AS i
    LEFT JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.ItemID = i.ItemID
WHERE i.SupplyMode = 'Manufactured' AND wo.WorkOrderID IS NULL;
```

The query returns a handful of manufactured items for which no work order has ever been released. Anti-joins are one of the most useful tests in accounting data, because they find what is missing: invoices never posted to the ledger, ledger rows that point to no document, and customers who have never ordered.

Two details of left joins cause most of the mistakes made with them. First, after a left join, `COUNT(*)` counts one row for an unmatched item. The item's row is still there, even though it has no work order. `COUNT(wo.WorkOrderID)` counts only the matches, and it returns zero for an item with no work orders, which is usually what you mean. Second, a condition on the second table placed in the WHERE clause turns a left join into an inner join. The condition `wo.Status = 'Closed'` in WHERE removes every item without a work order, because their Status is NULL. To keep those items, move the condition into the ON clause, where it limits which work orders are matched: `LEFT JOIN WorkOrder AS wo ON wo.ItemID = i.ItemID AND wo.Status = 'Closed'`.

::: {.callout-note .connecting-dots icon=false}
## Connecting the Dots
Chapter 3 warned that a list of customers built by joining to their orders can silently leave out the customers who have never ordered. That is the difference between an inner join and a left join. When the question is about every member of a population, such as every customer, item, or account, start from the table that holds the whole population and left join the others to it.
:::


## Fan-Out and Double Counting

A join between a header table and its lines returns one row per line, and it repeats the header's columns on every one of them. That is what you want when you need the header's date or customer beside each line. It is a trap when you add up an amount that belongs to the header. An invoice with three lines appears three times in a join of SalesInvoice and SalesInvoiceLine, and so does its GrandTotal. @fig-10-04 shows this effect, which is called fan-out, the double counting that Chapter 3 warned about when joining related tables. Summed over fiscal 2026, the join nearly doubles the invoice total.

![Fan-Out: A Header Amount Repeated on Every Line.](/visuals/svg/fig-10-04-fan-out.svg){#fig-10-04 fig-alt="A Charles River sales invoice of fiscal 2026 with three lines. Joined to its lines, the invoice's GrandTotal appears on all three rows, so summing GrandTotal over the join counts it three times, while summing the LineTotal of the lines counts each line once. A note states that across fiscal 2026 the sum of GrandTotal over the joined rows is nearly twice the true total of the invoices."}

The same effect appears whenever a join reaches from one table into another that has several rows for each of its rows. Each work order has three or four operations, so a query that joins work order closes to their operations, perhaps to see the work centers, repeats each close's variance three or four times. A sum of the variance over that join is several times the real figure.

The rule is to add up each amount at the level of the table it belongs to. Sum GrandTotal over SalesInvoice alone, and LineTotal over SalesInvoiceLine. When a question needs amounts from both levels, summarize the many side first, in a subquery, and then join the result to the one side, so that each row being joined represents one header. The next section shows how.


## Subqueries

A subquery is a query written inside another query, in parentheses. It lets you answer in one statement a question that takes two steps. A subquery in the WHERE clause usually supplies a value or a list for a condition. This query counts the closes of fiscal 2026 whose variance was above the year's average, which the subquery calculates first:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS AboveAverage
FROM WorkOrderClose
WHERE CloseDate BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'
    AND TotalVarianceAmount > (
        SELECT AVG(TotalVarianceAmount)
        FROM WorkOrderClose
        WHERE CloseDate BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31');
```

A subquery that returns a column can follow IN, as in `WHERE woc.WorkOrderID IN (SELECT wo.WorkOrderID FROM WorkOrder AS wo ...)`, which keeps the closes whose work order appears in the list.

A subquery in the FROM clause produces a table of its own, called a derived table, which the outer query can join and summarize like any other. It must have an alias. Derived tables are the way to combine results that are calculated at different levels, such as output summarized by year from one set of tables and hours summarized by year from another. Each is aggregated in its own subquery, and the two results are joined on the year. You will use this pattern in Tutorial 10.3.


## The Order in Which a Query Runs

A query is written in one order and evaluated in another. @fig-10-05 shows both. The database first assembles the rows from the tables in FROM and their joins. It then keeps the rows that meet the WHERE condition, forms the groups, and keeps the groups that meet the HAVING condition. Only then does it calculate the columns of the SELECT list. Finally, it sorts the result with ORDER BY and applies LIMIT.

![The Order in Which a Query Is Written and Evaluated.](/visuals/svg/fig-10-05-evaluation-order.svg){#fig-10-05 fig-alt="Two columns. The written order lists SELECT, FROM and JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, and LIMIT. The evaluation order lists FROM and JOIN first, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, and LIMIT, with a note beside each step on what it does, and lines connect each clause to its position in the other column."}

The evaluation order explains several rules you have already met. WHERE cannot use an aggregate, because the groups do not yet exist when WHERE runs. HAVING can, because it runs after grouping. ORDER BY can sort by an alias defined in the SELECT list, because it runs after SELECT. By the same logic, WHERE should not be able to use a column alias, and in most database systems it cannot. SQLite allows it, which is another habit to avoid if you want your queries to run elsewhere.

## The Purchasing, Manufacturing, and Payroll Tables

The questions of this Part reach beyond the sales and ledger tables of Part II, into the Procure-to-Pay and Manufacturing groups and the payroll. Chapter 3 described the Manufacturing group and introduced the others, and @fig-03-08 traced the tables of the manufacturing path, from the bill of materials to the close of a work order. @tbl-10-02 summarizes the joins you need to move through them. Each row names two tables and the key that links them, from the table that holds the foreign key to the table whose primary key it refers to.

| From | To | Join on |
|---|---|---|
| PurchaseOrderLine | PurchaseOrder | PurchaseOrderID |
| GoodsReceiptLine | PurchaseOrderLine | POLineID |
| PurchaseInvoiceLine | PurchaseOrderLine | POLineID |
| PurchaseInvoice | Supplier | SupplierID |
| DisbursementPayment | PurchaseInvoice | PurchaseInvoiceID |
| WorkOrder | Item | ItemID |
| WorkOrderOperation | WorkOrder | WorkOrderID |
| WorkOrderClose | WorkOrder | WorkOrderID |
| ProductionCompletionLine | ProductionCompletion | ProductionCompletionID |
| LaborTimeEntry | WorkOrderOperation | WorkOrderOperationID |
| PayrollRegisterLine | PayrollRegister | PayrollRegisterID |
| PayrollRegister | PayrollPeriod | PayrollPeriodID |

: Join paths through the purchasing, manufacturing, and payroll tables {#tbl-10-02}

Two of these tables carry more than one kind of row. LaborTimeEntry records direct labor against a work order operation, but it also records indirect manufacturing time, which is not charged to any work order and has no operation. A left join from LaborTimeEntry to WorkOrderOperation keeps both kinds, and the rows with no match are the indirect time. PayrollRegisterLine records regular and overtime earnings with their hours, but also salaries, employer taxes, benefits, and deductions, which have no hours. A filter on its LineType column chooses the lines a question needs.

These tables let you measure the plant the way a standard cost system does. A standard cost system compares the inputs actually used with the inputs the standards allow for the output actually achieved, such as the standard labor hours allowed for the units completed (Datar & Rajan, 2021). The hours paid come from the payroll, and the output and its standard hours come from the production completions and the Item table, so the comparison needs both sets of tables, summarized to the same period.

## Looking Ahead

This chapter has taught you to combine tables and summarize their rows. You joined tables with INNER JOIN on their logical keys and tested each join by its row count. You kept unmatched rows with LEFT JOIN and found missing records with anti-joins. You summarized with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX, grouped by key, filtered groups with HAVING, and avoided the double counting of fan-out. You wrote subqueries in WHERE and FROM, and you learned the order in which a query is evaluated. Along the way, you rebuilt the pre-closing trial balance of fiscal 2026 and followed the conversion cost of production through the ledger.

The controller now has her answer to the volume question, and it is not the one she expected. Output did not fall. The plant completed about as many units in fiscal 2026 as in fiscal 2024, and those units needed about as many standard labor hours. The payroll of the same people, however, paid for many more hours, and a growing share of them was overtime or time not charged to any work order. The actual conversion cost charged to production rose, while the standard cost that production absorbed stayed flat, and the difference is the variance. What the controller needs next is a measure she can follow month by month, one that shows whether the gap between paid hours and standard hours is still widening. Building that measure requires classifying rows, calculating across months, and organizing a long query into steps, which is the work of Chapter 11.
